subject: Career
title: Giving Before Asking: The Reciprocity Engine
description: A fast breakdown of Giving Before Asking: The Reciprocity Engine for builders.

hook.text: He helped a colleague get a speaking gig. Two years later, she referred him for his dream job.

buildup.text: Adam Grant's research shows 'givers' — people who help without expecting returns — are the most successful.

discovery.text: Every favor creates an implicit social debt. Help enough people and the returns surprise you.

twist.text: But not all giving is equal. Targeted generosity to people who can reciprocate is strategic, not selfish.

climax.text: Make a habit: introduce two people a week, share one useful resource, congratulate one achievement.

quiz.question: According to Adam Grant's research, who tends to be most successful?
options: Givers who help without expecting immediate returns

details.summary: Robert Cialdini's reciprocity principle shows that people feel obligated to return favors. In networking, consistently giving value before asking for anything creates a bank of goodwill that generates returns over years.
details.whyItMatters: Transactional networking burns out quickly. A give-first approach builds deep reciprocity reserves that produce opportunities long after the initial investment.
takeaways: Give three to five times before making any request of a new contact
Valuable gifts include introductions, knowledge, and recognition
Track your giving so the balance stays weighted toward generosity

faq.question: What are examples of valuable things to give in a professional network?
faq.answer: Make relevant introductions, share useful articles or tools, offer expertise on a problem they mentioned, amplify their work on social media, or provide a thoughtful recommendation. The best gifts cost you little but provide significant value to the recipient.

faq.question: Does the give-first approach work with very senior or busy people?
faq.answer: Especially well. Senior people are constantly asked for things and rarely offered value. A thoughtful give, like sharing a genuinely relevant insight or connecting them with someone they would not otherwise meet, stands out dramatically in their inbox.
